title: The Passive Voice
sub: When the action matters more than who did it — rice is grown, the law was passed.

uses.t: When the doer is unknown or unimportant
uses.d: The receiver of the action becomes the subject.
Passives put the topic first and keep the tone objective — common in reports and papers.

ex.s: Participants were asked to complete a survey.

uses.d: Mention the agent only when it adds real information.

ex.s: This novel was written by a local author.
The winning photo was taken by a student.

mistakes.no: The window was break by the wind.
mistakes.yes: The window was broken by the wind.
mistakes.why: Passive needs the past participle: broken.

mistakes.no: The cake eaten by the kids.
mistakes.yes: The cake was eaten by the kids.
mistakes.why: Never drop be — it carries the tense.

mistakes.no: He was gave a prize.
mistakes.yes: He was given a prize.
mistakes.why: Give → given after be.

tip: The tense lives in be, the meaning lives in the participle: is made → was made → has been made → will be made.

q.q: This bridge ___ over a century ago.
Bubble tea ___ all over the world now.
The email ___ (send) yesterday afternoon.
These photos ___ (take) by my grandfather.

q.sent: The report was written by the new intern
The package was deliver this morning .
Rice is grew in the south of Taiwan .

q.q: Which sentence is passive?
opts: The chef cooked a great meal.
q.why: Has been found = have + been + participle.

title: Relative Clauses
sub: Who, which, that, whose, where — folding two sentences into one.

ex: The woman who called is my boss.
The book that you lent me was great.

uses.d: Who for people, which for things, that for both (informal), whose for possession, where for places.

ex.s: The student who won the prize is in my class.
I lost the umbrella which / that you gave me.
That's the author whose book we're reading.

uses.d: The clause tells us which one — no commas.

ex.s: The train that leaves at six is always crowded.

uses.d: The clause just adds detail — use commas, and never that.

ex.s: My sister, who lives in Tainan, is visiting us.
ex.n: I have one sister; the clause is a bonus

mistakes.no: The man which fixed my car was kind.
mistakes.yes: The man who fixed my car was kind.
mistakes.why: People take who (or that), not which.

mistakes.no: The phone what I bought is fast.
mistakes.yes: The phone that I bought is fast.
mistakes.why: What is not a relative pronoun here.

mistakes.no: My mother, that is a nurse, works nights.
mistakes.yes: My mother, who is a nurse, works nights.
mistakes.why: After a comma, use who / which — never that.

tip: If you can delete the clause and still know exactly which thing you mean, it's non-defining: add commas and ban that.

q.q: The doctor ___ treated me was very patient.
This is the park ___ we used to play.
q.why: A place where something happens → where.

q.q: The artist ___ paintings sold out is only nineteen.
q.why: Whose shows the paintings belong to the artist.

q.q: I liked the gift ___ you chose. (thing; informal, one word)

q.sent: The movie that we watched was too long
The girl which sits next to me is from Korea .

q.q: Which sentence is correct?
opts: Taipei, that is huge, never sleeps.
Taipei, which is huge, never sleeps.
Taipei which is huge never sleeps.
Taipei, who is huge, never sleeps.

q.sent: He is the man who's car was stolen .
q.why: Possession uses whose; who's = who is.

title: Participle Clauses
sub: Feeling tired, she left early — trimming sentences with -ing and -ed.

uses.d: The subject of the main clause is doing the -ing action.

ex.s: Not knowing the answer, I stayed silent.

uses.d: The subject receives the action instead of doing it.

ex.s: Written in 1600, the play is still performed.
Surprised by the news, she sat down.
The cake, baked that morning, smelled amazing.

uses.d: Having + past participle marks an action that happened first.

ex.s: Having missed the bus, we took a taxi.
The typhoon hit at night, causing major delays.
Having lived in Tainan, she knows the food scene.

mistakes.no: Walking down the street, the trees looked beautiful.
mistakes.yes: Walking down the street, I saw beautiful trees.
mistakes.why: The -ing subject must match the main subject — trees don't walk. (A dangling participle!)

mistakes.no: Been tired, she went to bed.
mistakes.yes: Being tired, she went to bed.
mistakes.why: Active state → being.

mistakes.no: Having finish the work, he relaxed.
mistakes.yes: Having finished the work, he relaxed.
mistakes.why: Having + past participle.

tip: Ask: who is doing the -ing action? It must be the subject of the main clause — otherwise the sentence dangles.

q.q: ___ the door, she noticed a letter.
___ in Japan, the camera is high quality.
q.why: The camera was made → past participle.

q.q: ___ (finish) his homework, he went out to play.

q.sent: Wrote in a hurry , the essay had many mistakes .
q.why: The essay was written → past participle.

q.sent: Feeling hungry we stopped for noodles
q.why: V-ing phrase first, main clause after.

q.q: Which sentence dangles (is wrong)?
opts: Running to class, my bag broke.
Running to class, I dropped my bag.
Built last year, the bridge is new.
q.why: The bag wasn't running — the -ing subject must match.

q.q: ___ (not want) to be late, we left early.

q.sent: Having saw the movie twice , I skipped it .

title: Reported Speech
sub: Telling someone what another person said — and shifting the tense back.

uses.d: When the reporting verb is past (said, told), the original tense usually moves one step back.

ex.s: present simple → past: "I like it" → She said she liked it.
past simple → past perfect: "I saw him" → She said she had seen him.
will → would, can → could, must → had to

uses.d: Tell needs a person; say doesn't.
Questions lose their question order; requests use asked + to.

ex.s: "Where do you live?" → He asked where I lived.
"Are you okay?" → She asked if I was okay.

mistakes.no: She said me she was leaving.
mistakes.yes: She told me she was leaving.
mistakes.why: Say never takes a person directly — that's tell's job.

mistakes.no: He asked where did I work.
mistakes.yes: He asked where I worked.
mistakes.why: Reported questions use statement order.

mistakes.no: They said they will come.
mistakes.yes: They said they would come.
mistakes.why: After said, will shifts to would.

tip: Pronouns and time words shift with the tense: my → her, today → that day, tomorrow → the next day, here → there.

q.q: "I am hungry," he said. → He said he ___ hungry.
She ___ me that the meeting was cancelled.
"I will help you." → She said she ___ help me.
"Do you like jazz?" → He asked ___ I liked jazz.
q.why: Yes/no questions report with if or whether.

q.sent: He asked me where I had parked
q.why: Reported question → statement order, tense back.

q.sent: She said me that she felt sick .
q.why: Said + person is wrong — use told me.

q.sent: He asked what time did the show start .

q.q: "We saw the movie." → They said they ___ the movie.
q.why: Past simple shifts to past perfect.

title: Second Conditional
sub: Unreal or unlikely present and future — if I had a million dollars…

ex: If I had more time, I'd learn the violin.
If she lived closer, we'd meet more often.

uses.d: The past tense here doesn't mean past time — it signals this isn't real.

ex.s: If we didn't have exams, we'd travel this week.

uses.t: Advice with If I were you
uses.d: The classic advice formula — were is used for all persons in careful English.

ex.s: If I were you, I'd apologize first.
If I were him, I wouldn't sign that contract.

uses.t: First vs second: real vs unreal
uses.d: Choose by how likely you feel the condition is.

ex.s: If I have time tomorrow, I'll help. (real chance)
If I had time, I'd help. (but I don't)

mistakes.no: If I would have money, I'd travel.
mistakes.yes: If I had money, I'd travel.
mistakes.why: No would inside the if-clause.

mistakes.no: If she was you, she'd wait.
mistakes.yes: If she were you, she'd wait.
mistakes.why: Hypothetical be prefers were for all persons.

mistakes.no: If I won, I will quit my job.
mistakes.yes: If I won, I would quit my job.
mistakes.why: Unreal condition pairs with would, not will.

tip: Hear the pairing as a chord: past + would. If either half slips into present + will, you've changed the meaning to a real possibility.

q.q: If I ___ the lottery, I'd buy my parents a house.
If he spoke less, people ___ to him more.
If I ___ you, I'd take the offer. (be)
q.why: If I were you — hypothetical were.

q.q: She ___ travel more if she had longer holidays.

q.sent: If I had wings I would fly home
If I would know the answer , I'd tell you .
q.why: No would in the if-clause — use past simple.

q.q: Which is a second conditional?
opts: If you heat ice, it melts.
If I were rich, I'd donate more.

q.sent: If we lived by the sea , we will swim daily .

title: Third Conditional
sub: Rewriting the past that never happened — regrets, relief and lessons learned.

form.p: If + past perfect, … would have + participle
ex: She wouldn't have missed it if she'd left earlier.

uses.d: Both halves are 100% unreal — the past can't be changed.

ex.s: If you had told me, I would have helped.
ex.n: you didn't tell me, so I didn't help

ex.s: If the traffic hadn't been so bad, we would have arrived on time.
I would have taken the job if they'd offered more.

uses.d: Third conditionals carry strong feeling — what we wish had (not) happened.

ex.s: If I'd saved money in my twenties, I would have bought a flat.
If we'd taken that flight, we would have been stuck in the storm.

uses.t: Softer results: could have, might have
uses.d: Swap would for could or might when the result was possible, not certain.

ex.s: If she'd asked, I could have lent her mine.
If we'd left earlier, we might have caught the sunset.

mistakes.no: If I would have known, I'd have called.
mistakes.yes: If I had known, I'd have called.
mistakes.why: The if-clause takes past perfect, never would have.

mistakes.no: If she had asked, I would helped.
mistakes.yes: If she had asked, I would have helped.
mistakes.why: The result needs would have + participle.

mistakes.no: If we didn't miss the bus, we would have been early.
mistakes.yes: If we hadn't missed the bus, we would have been early.
mistakes.why: Unreal past condition → past perfect.

tip: Both clauses point at the same closed past: had + participle sets the scene, would have + participle imagines the outcome.

q.q: If you ___ me, I would have picked you up.
She ___ the deadline if her laptop hadn't crashed.
If I had seen the sign, I ___ have parked there. (negative)
If they ___ (leave) earlier, they would have caught the train.

q.sent: If I had known I would have waited
If I would have studied , I'd have passed .
q.why: If-clause: had studied, never would have.

q.sent: If she had asked , I would helped her .

q.q: "If we'd booked earlier, we might have gotten seats." What really happened?
opts: They booked early and got seats.
They didn't book early and didn't get seats.
q.why: Third conditional describes an unreal past — the opposite happened.

title: Noun Clauses & the Subjunctive
sub: That she left, whether it works — clauses that act like nouns, plus the demand-verb pattern.

form.p: verb + that / whether / if + clause   ·   suggest that + subject + base verb
ex: They insisted that he be on time.

uses.d: A whole clause can be the thing you know, say or believe.

ex.s: Everyone believes that the plan will work.

ex.n: that is often dropped in speech

ex.s: The problem is that we have no budget.

uses.d: When the inner question is a yes-no question, use whether or if.

ex.s: I don't know whether he got the message.
Whether we win or lose, we tried our best.
ex.n: whether can start a sentence; if can't here

uses.d: Suggest, insist, demand, recommend, require + that → base verb.

ex.s: It is essential that every student bring ID.

mistakes.no: I suggested that he goes home.
mistakes.yes: I suggested that he go home.
mistakes.why: After suggest that, the verb stays in base form.

mistakes.no: I don't know that he will come or not.
mistakes.yes: I don't know whether he will come or not.
mistakes.why: Or not pairs with whether.

mistakes.no: It is important that she is on time.
mistakes.yes: It is important that she be on time.
mistakes.why: The demand pattern uses the base verb be.

tip: Demand-type verbs (suggest, insist, recommend, demand, require) + that → base verb, even for he / she / it.

q.q: The teacher insisted that every student ___ the meeting.
I'm not sure ___ the store is open today.
She suggested that he ___ (see) a doctor.

q.sent: We demanded that the company refunds our money .
I wonder whether she got my message

q.q: Which is correct?
opts: It is vital that he is here by nine.
It is vital that he be here by nine.
It is vital that he being here by nine.
It is vital that he to be here by nine.

q.q: He told me ___ he had already eaten.

q.sent: I asked her that she was free on Sunday .
q.why: A yes-no question inside → whether or if.

title: Wish: Present
sub: Wishing the present were different — I wish I had more time.

form.p: wish + past simple (for now) · wish + could + base verb

uses.t: wish + past simple = a different present
uses.d: Use wish + the past simple to wish that a present situation were different. It is NOT true now.
With the verb be, use 'were' for every subject in careful English.

uses.t: wish + could = an ability we don't have
uses.d: Use wish + could + base verb to wish for an ability or possibility.

mistakes.no: I wish I have more time.
mistakes.yes: I wish I had more time.
mistakes.why: After wish (about now), use the past simple: had.

mistakes.no: I wish I can fly.
mistakes.yes: I wish I could fly.
mistakes.why: Use 'could' (not 'can') after wish.

mistakes.no: I wish I will be rich.
mistakes.yes: I wish I were rich.
mistakes.why: For a present wish, use the past (were), not 'will'.

tip: wish + past simple = wanting the present to be different (I wish I had… = but I don't). With be, use 'were'. For ability, use 'wish + could'.

q.q: I wish I ___ a bigger house. (but I don't)
She wishes she ___ taller. (be)
I wish I ___ play the guitar. (an ability I don't have)
It's so noisy. I wish it ___ quiet. (be, present wish)
I don't know the answer. I wish I ___ . (know, present wish)

q.sent: I wish I lived near you
q.why: wish + past simple (lived) = but I don't.

q.sent: I wish I can speak Japanese .

q.q: 'I wish I had a dog' means…
opts: I don't have a dog, but I want one.
q.why: wish + past = it's not true now; I want it.

title: Gerunds & Infinitives
sub: Enjoy swimming but decide to swim — which verb takes which form?

uses.d: Enjoy, finish, avoid, keep, mind, suggest, practice — these take -ing.
Want, decide, hope, plan, promise, offer, learn, need — these take to + verb.

ex.s: We plan to visit Alishan in autumn.

uses.t: Verbs that take both — with a twist
uses.d: Some verbs change meaning: remember, stop, try, forget.

ex.s: I stopped drinking coffee. (= quit the habit)
I stopped to drink some water. (= paused in order to drink)
Remember to lock the door. (a task ahead) · I remember locking it. (a memory)

mistakes.no: I enjoy to swim.
mistakes.yes: I enjoy swimming.
mistakes.why: Enjoy always takes the gerund.

mistakes.no: She wants going home.
mistakes.yes: She wants to go home.
mistakes.why: Want always takes the infinitive.

mistakes.no: He avoided to answer.
mistakes.yes: He avoided answering.
mistakes.why: Avoid takes the gerund.

tip: A rough compass: gerunds often look back or describe habits (enjoy, finish, avoid); infinitives often look forward (want, plan, hope, decide).

q.q: She avoided ___ my question.
They decided ___ a new apartment.
I really enjoy ___ (cook) on weekends.
He hopes ___ (pass) the IELTS next month.

q.sent: She suggested going to the museum instead
I finished to read the novel last night .

q.q: "I stopped to buy milk" means…
opts: I paused my journey in order to buy milk.
q.why: Stop + infinitive = pause in order to do something.

q.sent: Remember locking the door before you leave tonight .

title: Phrasal Verbs
sub: Take off, put up with, run into — small words, big meaning changes.

uses.t: Separable: the object can split them
uses.d: Noun objects can go in the middle or after; pronouns MUST go in the middle.

ex.s: Please turn off the light. / Please turn the light off.
Write down the address before you forget.

uses.d: Some phrasal verbs never split — the object always follows.

ex.s: I ran into Mrs. Chen at the market.
We need to look after the neighbor's cat.

uses.d: Verb + two particles — these never split either.

ex.s: I can't put up with the noise anymore.

mistakes.no: She picked up it.
mistakes.yes: She picked it up.
mistakes.why: Pronoun objects go between the verb and the particle.

mistakes.no: He looks after very well his dog.
mistakes.yes: He looks after his dog very well.
mistakes.why: Don't split inseparable phrasal verbs.

mistakes.no: I will put up the noise with.
mistakes.yes: I will put up with the noise.
mistakes.why: Three-part phrasal verbs never split.

tip: Learn each phrasal verb as one word with its own meaning — give up has nothing to do with giving.

q.q: Can you turn ___ the music? It's too loud.
I ran ___ my old teacher at the MRT station.
We've run out ___ milk — I'll buy some.
q.why: Run out of = have none left.

q.sent: He gave in smoking last year .
I will look after your cat this weekend

q.q: “Turn down” in “turn down an offer” means…
q.why: Turn down an offer = refuse it.

q.q: Don't give ___ — you're almost there!

q.sent: She looks up at her coach as a role model .

title: Modals of Deduction
sub: Must have, might have, can't have — reading the clues about the past and present.

form.p: modal + base verb (present)   ·   modal + have + p.p. (past)

uses.d: How sure are you about right now?

ex.s: The lights are on — someone must be home.

uses.d: The same logic pointed at the past.

ex.s: The ground is wet — it must have rained.
She isn't here; she might have gone home.
He can't have finished already — it's too soon.

uses.t: Regret and criticism: should have, needn't have
uses.d: Judging past choices — yours or someone else's.

ex.n: you didn't — and that was a mistake

ex.s: We needn't have hurried — the train was late.
ex.n: we hurried, but it wasn't necessary

mistakes.no: He must had left.
mistakes.yes: He must have left.
mistakes.why: Modal + have + past participle — have never changes.

mistakes.no: You should have call me.
mistakes.yes: You should have called me.
mistakes.why: Have + past participle.

mistakes.no: She mustn't have seen us.
mistakes.yes: She can't have seen us.
mistakes.why: For “surely not” about the past, use can't have.

tip: Sure it happened → must have. Maybe → might / could have. Surely not → can't have.

q.q: The streets are wet. It ___ rained.
He knows every scene of the movie — he ___ seen it.
I failed the test. I ___ have studied harder.

q.sent: She must has forgotten our meeting .
q.why: After a modal, have never changes.

q.sent: He might have taken the early train
q.why: Maybe about the past → might have + p.p.

q.q: “We needn't have booked” means…
opts: We booked, but it wasn't necessary.
q.why: Needn't have = did it, but it wasn't needed.

q.q: That ___ be Lisa at the door — she's in Japan!

q.sent: You should have wake me up earlier .

zh: 字首 un- / re- / im- / in-
title: Prefixes: un-, re-, im-/in-
sub: Small beginnings that change a word's meaning — 'not' and 'again'.

uses.d: These make a word negative. Use im- before m/p, il- before l, ir- before r; in- or un- otherwise.
re- means to do something again.
Just add the prefix — don't drop or double letters (some words keep a double letter).

mistakes.no: He is inpolite.
mistakes.yes: He is impolite.
mistakes.why: Before p (and m), use im-: impolite.

mistakes.no: That's unpossible.
mistakes.yes: That's impossible.
mistakes.why: The opposite of possible is impossible (im-).

mistakes.no: That noise is unecessary.
mistakes.yes: That noise is unnecessary.
mistakes.why: un + necessary keeps both n's: unnecessary.

tip: un- / in- / im- / il- / ir- all mean 'not'. re- means 'again'. Keep the base word's spelling — don't drop letters.

q.q: The opposite of 'happy' is ___.
'Please ___ your work' (= write it again).
The opposite of 'possible' is ___.
He was very ___patient while waiting. (not patient)
The opposite of 'correct' is ___correct.

q.sent: This rule is unregular .

q.q: 're-' in 'rebuild' means…

q.sent: That homework is unecessary .

title: Suffixes: -er, -able, -ness
sub: Small endings that turn a word into a person, a describing word or an idea.

uses.t: -er = a person or thing that does something
uses.d: Add -er to a verb to make the doer.
Add -able to a verb to make an adjective meaning 'can be done'.

uses.t: -ness = an idea or quality (makes a noun)
uses.d: Add -ness to an adjective to make an abstract noun.

mistakes.no: She is a good teach.
mistakes.yes: She is a good teacher.
mistakes.why: A person who teaches is a teacher (+ -er).

mistakes.no: I want happyness.
mistakes.yes: I want happiness.
mistakes.why: happy → happiness (y → i before -ness).

mistakes.no: This chair is very comfort.
mistakes.yes: This chair is very comfortable.
mistakes.why: Comfort (noun) → comfortable (adjective).

tip: -er makes the doer (teach → teacher). -able makes an adjective 'can be…' (enjoy → enjoyable). -ness makes an idea-noun (kind → kindness). Watch spelling: y → i, drop silent e.

q.q: A person who sings is a ___.
'happy' + '-ness' = ___.
Something you can enjoy is ___.
kind + -ness = ___ .
q.why: kindness = the quality of being kind.

q.q: A person who drives is a ___ .

q.sent: This bottle is breakible .

q.q: '-ness' turns an adjective into a…

q.sent: He shows great kindess .
